[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental analysis of H-1B visa lottery outcomes linked to patent data and metropolitan wage records (e.g., using data from USPTO, ACS, and LEHD) — This would allow causal identification of the effect of high-skilled immigrant inflows on native wages in high-patenting metros, while testing the condition that immigrants and natives are in the same broad industry sector.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of studies on skill complementarity and immigrant-native wage effects in innovation-intensive cities (e.g., Peri, Sparber, Kerr, Hunt) — Existing empirical work often finds positive wage effects for native workers with complementary skills, but the specific moderating role of same-sector employment and high patenting activity is less tested; a systematic review could confirm or challenge the conditional nature of the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of labor market matching in urban innovation clusters (e.g., search-and-matching models with heterogeneous skills and sectoral spillovers) — A model can clarify the mechanisms through which high-skilled immigrants in the same sector as natives raise native wages in patent-intensive metros, and identify conditions under which the effect might vanish or reverse, guiding further empirical tests.

C006.object: in metropolitan areas with high patenting activity

[PATH:empirical] Analysis of U.S. Census Bureau and American Community Survey microdata linked to patent data from the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) for metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) with high patenting activity post-2000, using a shift-share instrumental variable approach to isolate causal effects of high-skilled immigration on native wages. — This quasi-experimental design can directly test the hypothesis by comparing wage changes for native workers in high-patent MSAs with varying inflows of high-skilled immigrants, controlling for local labor demand shocks.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on high-skilled immigration and native wages, focusing on heterogeneous effects across skill levels and geographic areas (e.g., Peri, 2012; Kerr & Lincoln, 2010; Borjas, 2003). — Synthesizing prior empirical findings can reveal whether the predicted negative wage effect is consistently observed in innovation-intensive metros or if complementarity effects (e.g., increased innovation and productivity) dominate, thereby refuting the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural labor market model calibrated to U.S. data, incorporating skill heterogeneity, firm-level innovation, and local labor market competition due to high-skilled immigration in patent-intensive areas. — A theoretical model can clarify the conditions under which increased competition from high-skilled immigrants reduces native wages (e.g., perfect substitutability) versus raises them (e.g., through innovation spillovers), guiding empirical tests and resolving the disputed status.

[PATH:empirical] Panel microdata from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) linked to patent data from the USPTO and firm-level market concentration measures (e.g., HHI from Compustat) for metropolitan areas, 2010-2023 — This would allow a difference-in-differences or instrumental-variable analysis to test whether high-skilled immigration depresses wages for native workers with overlapping skills only in MSAs where the innovation sector is dominated by large incumbent firms, directly addressing the conditional effect in the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of labor market monopsony and innovation, such as those in 'Labor Market Concentration' (Berger, Herkenhoff, Mongey, 2022) and 'Immigration and the Labor Market: A Review' (Dustmann, Schönberg, Stuhler, 2016), extended to incorporate firm size distribution and patenting activity — Developing a model where large incumbent firms have market power in the labor market for high-skilled workers can clarify the mechanism through which immigration depresses wages only under such conditions, providing testable predictions and supporting causal interpretation of empirical findings.

[PATH:literature] Literature on high-skilled immigration and innovation: e.g., 'The Impact of High-Skilled Immigration on Firm Innovation' (Kerr, Lincoln, 2010) and 'Immigration and the Rise of American Ingenuity' (Akcigit, Grigsby, Nicholas, 2017), combined with studies on market concentration (e.g., 'The Fall of the Labor Share and the Rise of Superstar Firms' by Autor et al., 2020) — A systematic review of existing empirical and theoretical work can identify whether prior studies have found heterogeneous wage effects by firm concentration, and whether the hypothesized interaction between high-skilled immigration, patenting activity, and incumbent firm dominance is supported or contradicted by available evidence, thus helping to confirm or refute the hypothesis.
